title: Rutledge v. Clearway Energy Group LLC
description: Whether Senate Bill 21, which amends the Delaware General Corporation Law to establish safe harbor provisions for controlling-stockholder transactions and applies retroactively, violates the Delaware Constitution by divesting the Court of Chancery of its equitable jurisdiction or eliminating accrued causes of action.
plaintiff_argument: The plaintiff, Thomas Drew Rutledge, argued that SB 21's safe harbor provisions unconstitutionally divest the Court of Chancery of its equitable jurisdiction and that its retroactive application unconstitutionally eliminates vested causes of action.
defendant_argument: The defendants, Clearway Energy Group LLC, Christopher Sotos, Clearway Energy, Inc., and the State of Delaware, argued that SB 21 provides a statutory review framework without reducing the Court of Chancery's jurisdiction and that the General Assembly has the constitutional authority to enact such legislation, which does not extinguish vested rights.
decision_outcome: The court ruled that Senate Bill 21 is constitutional, affirming the General Assembly's power to enact the amendments and their retroactive application.

title: In re Covid-related Restrictions on Religious Services
description: Whether the Governor's COVID-19 restrictions on religious services violated constitutional rights, as argued by the plaintiffs, or if the Governor was immune from suit and the claims were non-justiciable, as argued by the defendant.
plaintiff_argument: The Governor's COVID-19 restrictions on religious services violated their constitutional rights, including free exercise, free speech, free assembly, free association, establishment clause, and equal protection, and the Governor was not immune from suit.
defendant_argument: The restrictions were a necessary exercise of his discretionary authority under the Emergency Management Act to protect public health, and he is immune from suit under the State Tort Claims Act and qualified immunity, making the claims non-justiciable because the restrictions were lifted and the threat of future harm was speculative.
decision_outcome: The Supreme Court affirmed the lower courts' decisions to dismiss the plaintiffs' claims, finding them non-justiciable and the Governor immune from suit.

title: Albence v. Mennella
description: Whether Delaware's Permanent-Absentee Statute and Early-Voting Laws violate the state constitution by expanding absentee voting eligibility and in-person voting beyond the constitutionally designated election day.
plaintiff_argument: The plaintiffs argued that the Permanent-Absentee Statute violates Article V, § 4A by granting indefinite absentee voting eligibility, and the Early-Voting Laws violate Article V, § 1 by expanding in-person voting beyond the constitutionally designated election day, leading to vote dilution.
defendant_argument: The defendants argued that the plaintiffs lacked standing to challenge the statutes because they failed to demonstrate a concrete, particularized, and imminent injury, and that the statutes are constitutional.
decision_outcome: The Supreme Court reversed the Superior Court's judgment, vacated its declaratory judgment, and dismissed the plaintiffs' amended complaint for lack of standing, thereby allowing the challenged statutes to remain in effect.

title: Burroughs v. State
description: Whether the Delaware bail system, which allows for unaffordable financial conditions for pretrial release, violates the Equal Protection Clause, Substantive and Procedural Due Process, and the state constitutional right to bail, with the plaintiff arguing it is unconstitutional and the defendant arguing it is permissible and necessary for public safety.
plaintiff_argument: Tyrese Burroughs argued that the imposition of unaffordable cash bail for pretrial release violates his federal constitutional rights to equal protection and due process, and his state constitutional right to bail, contending he should have been released without financial conditions.
defendant_argument: The State of Delaware argued that the bail system is constitutional, that Burroughs posed a serious safety risk to the community, and that unaffordable cash bail was a necessary and permissible condition to ensure public safety and his appearance in court.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed the Superior Court's judgment, holding that Delaware's bail system does not violate the Equal Protection or Due Process Clauses of the Fourteenth Amendment, nor Article I, § 12 of the Delaware Constitution, provided that cash bail for pretrial detention is supported by clear and convincing evidence and procedural protections are observed.

title: State v. Higgin
description: Whether the Same-Day Registration Statute and the Vote-by-Mail Statute are constitutional under the Delaware Constitution, with plaintiffs arguing they violate constitutional provisions and defendants arguing they are valid exercises of legislative power.
plaintiff_argument: The plaintiffs contended that the Same-Day Registration Statute conflicts with Article V, Section 4, and the Vote-by-Mail Statute conflicts with Article V, Section 4A, of the Delaware Constitution.
defendant_argument: The defendants argued that the plaintiffs lacked standing and, even if they had standing, the laws were within the General Assembly's plenary power and therefore valid.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed the invalidation of the Vote-by-Mail Statute and reversed the lower court's decision on the Same-Day Registration Statute, concluding that both laws violate the Delaware Constitution.

title: In re Opinion of the Justices
description: Whether Article III, Section 13 of the Delaware Constitution, concerning the removal of public officials by the Governor upon address of the General Assembly, allows for lesser actions like suspension, considers an indictment alone as reasonable cause, and requires specific hearing procedures and notice.
plaintiff_argument: The General Assembly sought clarification, potentially hoping for broader interpretations of their powers, such as allowing suspension as a lesser action, considering an indictment as sufficient reasonable cause, and flexibility in hearing procedures.
defendant_argument: The court clarified that the Governor's authority under Section 13 does not include suspension, an indictment alone is not sufficient for "reasonable cause," and specific hearing and notice requirements (including due process elements) are mandatory.
decision_outcome: The Supreme Court provided an advisory opinion to the General Assembly, clarifying that under Article III, Section 13, "reasonable cause" for removal may include an indictment but an indictment alone is insufficient, the authority to remove does not include suspension, a hearing is required prior to a vote on a bill of address (which can be in the first House or joint), and specific due process elements must be afforded during the hearing. There is no appeal from the Governor's decision.
